reading_md:
## Comparing a period with another period

Managers ask "how did this month do?" A number on its own says little; next to the month before, or the same month last year, it tells a story. The pattern has two steps:

1. **Add up to the period first**: one row per month (or week, or quarter), in a CTE.
2. **Put the other period beside each row**, then work out the change.

### The previous period: LAG

`LAG(revenue_eur) OVER (ORDER BY month)` reads the row before. That is the month before only when every month has a row. If a month had no orders, the row before is two months back. A full list of periods fixes that (the next lesson, date spines).

### The same period last year: join on the date

`LAG(revenue_eur, 12)` counts twelve rows back, not twelve months. One missing month in the year before shifts every comparison after it (`ERR-LOG-39`). A join on the date cannot shift:

```sql
FROM monthly m
LEFT JOIN monthly p ON p.month = m.month - INTERVAL 1 YEAR
```

LEFT JOIN keeps a 2025 month whose 2024 month had no orders, with a missing value. The question decides whether such a month shows missing or 0.

### Direction and scale

- The change is this period minus the earlier one: revenue that goes from 100 to 120 rose by 20.
- Growth divides by the **earlier** period: `100.0 * (this - last) / last` gives 20.0. Dividing by this period gives 16.7, and the other order gives -20 (`ERR-LOG-49`).
- 12.5 and 0.125 are the same growth on scales 100 apart; give the scale the question asks for (`ERR-LOG-21`).

### Partial periods and like for like

Data stops on the day it is pulled. December so far (1 to 14 December) against all of November looks like a fall that is only the missing days (`ERR-LOG-48`). Compare the same days of both months, or leave the partial month out.

Stores work the same way: a store that opened in September 2024 sold for four months that year, so its 2025 "growth" is mostly its extra months. A like-for-like comparison keeps only stores open for the whole of both periods.

### WHERE runs before the window

Filter to 2025 before LAG and January has no December to read. Work the comparison out over the wider range in a CTE, then keep the rows you report.
syntax_md:
```sql
WITH monthly AS (                               -- source: one row per month
  SELECT order_month AS month, SUM(net_revenue_eur) AS revenue_eur
  FROM sales
  GROUP BY order_month
)
SELECT m.month, m.revenue_eur,
  m.revenue_eur - LAG(m.revenue_eur) OVER (ORDER BY m.month) AS change_eur,  -- the row before
  p.revenue_eur AS revenue_prev_year_eur                                     -- a year before
FROM monthly m
LEFT JOIN monthly p ON p.month = m.month - INTERVAL 1 YEAR;                   -- found by date
```

- Change: this period minus the earlier one. Growth in percent: `100.0 * (this - last) / last`.
- LAG reads the row before; it is the period before only when no period is missing.
- For last year, join on the date (or on the year minus 1 and the same month number).
- Compare the same number of days, and the same stores, in both periods.
dialect_note: LAG and the self-join are standard SQL. `m.month - INTERVAL 1 YEAR` runs in DuckDB and PostgreSQL; BigQuery writes `DATE_SUB(month, INTERVAL 1 YEAR)`. Matching on the year minus 1 and the same month number works on every engine.

worked_examples.title: Month-over-month change in units
worked_examples.prompt: For each month of 2025, show the units Voltmarkt sold and the change from the previous calendar month, this month minus last month. Every month of 2025 has orders; January shows a missing change.

clauses.text: WITH monthly AS (SELECT order_month AS month, SUM(units) AS units FROM sales WHERE order_date BETWEEN DATE '2025-01-01' AND DATE '2025-12-31' GROUP BY order_month)  -- one row per month of 2025
clauses.why: Add up to one row per month first; the comparison works on months, not order lines.
Every month keeps its own row and total.

clauses.text: units - LAG(units) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS change_units
clauses.why: LAG reads the month before in month order; this month minus it is the change, missing for January.
One row per month, and every month of 2025 is there, so the row before is the month before.

worked_examples.title: Year over year with a self-join
worked_examples.prompt: For each month of 2025 with ad spend, show Mailvora's spend and the spend of the same month of 2024, missing when that month of 2024 had none.

clauses.text: WITH monthly AS (SELECT CAST(date_trunc('month', spend_date) AS DATE) AS month, SUM(spend) AS spend_eur FROM ad_spend_daily GROUP BY CAST(date_trunc('month', spend_date) AS DATE))  -- one row per month with spend
clauses.why: One row per month with spend, over both years, so last year is there to join to.

clauses.text: SELECT m.month, m.spend_eur, p.spend_eur AS spend_prev_year_eur
clauses.why: The 2025 month's spend beside the spend of the month it matched a year before.

clauses.text: LEFT JOIN monthly p ON p.month = m.month - INTERVAL 1 YEAR
clauses.why: Matched by date, so a missing month cannot shift the series; LEFT keeps a month with no 2024 match.
Report 2025 only; the 2024 rows were needed for the join, not for the output.

why_clause.clause: LEFT JOIN monthly p ON p.month = m.month - INTERVAL 1 YEAR
why_clause.stem: Why join on the month minus one year instead of reading LAG(spend_eur, 12)?

options.text: LAG 12 counts rows, so one month with no spend makes it read the wrong month; the join finds last year by its date.
LAG cannot read more than one row back.
The join is faster, and both give the same rows on any data.
LAG 12 would count the months of 2025 twice.

why_clause.explanation: LAG(x, 12) reads twelve rows back, which is twelve months back only when every month has a row. If a month had no spend, twelve rows back lands on another month. The date join matches the exact month a year earlier, and LEFT JOIN keeps a month with no match as missing. LAG can read any number of rows back; the two differ exactly when a month is missing.
